# ID: Identity

*Generated by `tools/ssp/build.py`. Edit its sources, not this page.*

## ID-1: Identity Platform and Management

KESTREL's identity design rests on Active Directory in the mission data center. It is the source of truth for who people are, and Microsoft Entra ID carries a copy of it into the cloud. Because the directory controls access to every boundary, KESTREL protects it as its most valuable asset. The outcomes below follow a person's identity through its life. It starts on the day they are proofed and enrolled, runs through the access they are granted and reviewed for, and ends when their account is retired.

### ID-1.1: Identity Proofing and Enrollment

KESTREL will proof every person before issuing an account, at the assurance level the AMP sets for their population. For DoD users and performers, most of that work is already done. DoD proofed them to issue their CAC, which also confirmed their address. KESTREL will bind each account to that CAC record instead of proofing the person a second time. The program office's sponsorship of each performer's CAC doubles as the nomination KESTREL requires.

Partners and vendors are different, since they hold no CAC. A KESTREL sponsor will attest to each one instead. Either way, IT Operations records the enrollment in Jira Service Management, and Entra ID Governance creates the baseline account once enrollment is complete. Two attributes keep these populations distinguishable later on. CAC affiliation marks contractors, while a nationality attribute marks partners.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-12, IA-12(1), IA-12(2), IA-12(3), IA-4, IA-4(4), AC-2(1), IA-12(5). SIP record: [ID-1.1](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-11-identity-proofing-and-enrollment). Details: the AMP, [Section 1](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#1-identity-proofing-and-population-management) and [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-1.2: External PKI Trust and Sponsorship

Two kinds of outsiders will sign in with certificates KESTREL does not issue. Vendor support engineers come first. They will connect from the first build, on External Certificate Authority credentials at the Medium Hardware level, and each vendor identity will reach only its own support cases.

Coalition partners follow in Phase 3, once integration testing under the interim authorization to test is finished. Their systems will present certificates from their own nation's PKI or an ECA, and KESTREL will trust them only for the partner API that Mission Team 2 runs. Every partner has a named KESTREL sponsor, and every external credential is checked for revocation at each session. Because the trust list names each partner nation's issuing authorities, adding a new partner nation is significant enough to trigger a CCSD revision.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-8, IA-8(1), IA-8(2), IA-8(4), IA-8(5), IA-12(6), IA-5(2), AC-2. SIP record: [ID-1.2](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-12-external-pki-trust-and-sponsorship). Details: the AMP, [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-1.3: Centralized Identity Platform

KESTREL's identities will live in Active Directory in the mission data center, with a warm standby at the alternate site. Entra Connect Sync copies the directory into Entra ID, which then handles federation and access policy for everything in the cloud. Each team's identities sit in their own organizational unit, mirrored in Entra ID as an administrative unit, so one team's administrators cannot touch another's accounts.

Putting the system of record on premises was a choice made with the fleet in mind. If the cloud becomes unreachable, directory logon still works, the stations still check CACs locally, and the break-glass accounts still open. Only cloud-federated sign-in has to wait for the circuit to come back.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-2, AC-2. SIP record: [ID-1.3](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-13-centralized-identity-platform).</sub>

### ID-1.4: Identity Platform Threat Detection and Hardening

The identity provider controls access to every boundary in KESTREL, so it will be monitored more closely than any other system. Defender for Identity covers the domain controllers in the data center and at the alternate site. In the cloud, Entra ID Protection does the same job for sign-ins. Both send their alerts to Splunk Enterprise Security, where the Security Team and the CSSP see them alongside every other source.

Alongside that monitoring, the directory will be hardened to its DISA STIG, and Entra ID to the cloud provider's IL5 baseline for the identity service.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: SI-4(2), CM-6. SIP record: [ID-1.4](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-14-identity-platform-threat-detection-and-hardening).</sub>

### ID-1.5: Directory and Tier 0 Infrastructure Hardening

KESTREL's root certificate authority will stay offline and off the domain, with its key held in the nShield HSMs. It is used only in two-person ceremonies, which sign the issuing authorities and their revocation lists.

Below the root, the issuing authorities, domain controllers, and directory sync servers are all treated as Tier 0, both in the data center and at the alternate site's standby. Synchronization to the cloud runs only over the dedicated circuit. Within Tier 0, the aim is that no system depends on a password someone could remember. Windows LAPS rotates the local administrator passwords for that reason, and group Managed Service Accounts run the directory's own services.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: CM-6, IA-5. SIP record: [ID-1.5](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-15-directory-and-tier-0-infrastructure-hardening). Details: the AMP, [Section 3](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#3-credential-and-secret-rotation).</sub>

### ID-1.6: Third-Party Application and SaaS Access Governance

Only one SaaS service will be admitted to KESTREL's identities, and that is its own Microsoft 365 DoD tenant. Even that goes through intake and needs an administrator's consent. User consent is switched off at the Entra tenant, so no individual can grant an application access to their account. The foundation model is a separate case. The cloud provider hosts it inside KESTREL's tenant and it receives no delegated user access, so it is not treated as a third-party application at all.

Because KESTREL allows almost no general egress, finding any other service is mostly a matter of watching the egress allow-list. Defender for Cloud Apps will do that from the egress logs of both hubs and the alternate site's firewall, which covers every location.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-3(12), SI-4(2). SIP record: [ID-1.6](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-16-third-party-application-and-saas-access-governance).</sub>

### ID-1.7: Identities and Entitlements Lifecycle

Access will be granted through role bundles. Each user role in the system description gets an entitlement bundle, scoped to the team that role belongs to. An analyst's bundle, for example, reaches their own mission team's raw collection and detections, plus the shared reports every team can read. Approving an AI agent's work is part of a bundle too. Operators approve the mission-planning agent's drafts, and developers' reviewers approve the coding agent's merge requests.

Every change goes through a recorded request. Active Directory groups own membership for each role, and IT Operations changes them only through Jira Service Management. The approval itself comes from the requester's product owner or team lead, which keeps anyone from both approving and provisioning the same access. Entra ID Governance access packages fill the gap for the few resources that exist only in the cloud.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-2, AC-2(6), AC-6. SIP record: [ID-1.7](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-17-identities-and-entitlements-lifecycle). Details: the AMP, [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-1.8: Account Lifecycle and Identity Data Quality

KESTREL will retire each account when the person no longer needs it. When someone leaves, IT Operations disables their Active Directory account and revokes their CAC binding, and the change flows through to Entra ID on its own. The ground control stations pick up the revocation at their daily refresh, and again before each flight. Partner accounts, meanwhile, expire along with their sponsor's agreement.

Dormant accounts are handled separately. Each day Splunk will work out who has gone quiet, using Active Directory, Entra ID, and station sign-ins. Ansible Automation Platform then disables anyone dormant past the AMP's threshold. Break-glass accounts are excluded, since they are meant to stay unused.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-2(1), AC-2(3), IA-4. SIP record: [ID-1.8](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-18-account-lifecycle-and-identity-data-quality). Details: the AMP, [Section 4](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#4-account-lifecycle).</sub>

### ID-1.9: Access Reviews

From Phase 2, access will be recertified on the AMP's cadence. Operators, platform administrators, and partners will be reviewed more often than analysts, because their access carries more risk.

The Security Team's ISSM owns the reviews, while the Platform Team runs the tools behind them. Entra ID Governance handles campaigns for cloud and directory access, and CyberArk's own reviews cover the vaulted privileged accounts. The people who know whether access is still needed take part directly. Each partner review includes its sponsor, and each operator review includes Fleet Operations' operations lead.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-6(7), AC-2, AC-2(7). SIP record: [ID-1.9](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-19-access-reviews). Details: the AMP, [Section 6](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#6-access-review).</sub>

### ID-1.10: Physical and Logical Access Convergence

KESTREL will connect where someone physically is with what they are signed in to. The PSO runs the physical access control systems at the data center and each operating site, and the parent organization's facility runs the one at the alternate site. KESTREL does not operate any of them. Instead, from Phase 2, its account lifecycle events will drive the PSO's badge provisioning and removal, so a departure removes a badge as well as an account.

In Phase 3, when the fleet's logs arrive, Splunk Enterprise Security will compare badge events with sign-ins. An operator who is signed in at a station without having badged into that site will raise an alert.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: PE-3, PE-2, AC-2, AU-6(6). SIP record: [ID-1.10](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-110-physical-and-logical-access-convergence).</sub>

## ID-2: User Identity Protection

This capability covers how people prove their identity and what that identity lets them do. In nearly every case, KESTREL users will authenticate with a smart card, whether a CAC, an ECA credential, or a partner nation's PKI card. Access then depends on role and team, and it keeps being checked against device posture and risk for as long as a session lasts. The ground control stations follow the same rules, with a few deliberate exceptions where a locked console could put an aircraft at risk.

### ID-2.1: User Authentication Controls

Every person will authenticate with a certificate on a smart card. Cloud sign-in runs through Entra certificate-based authentication, and on-premises logon through Active Directory smart cards. Passwords survive in only two places. Built-in accounts that CyberArk vaults and injects are one, and the break-glass accounts under Emergency Access are the other.

The ground control stations need two adjustments. First, each station checks the CAC locally against a cached revocation list, so a station keeps working when its conduit is down. Second, a station whose aircraft is airborne will never lock an account after failed logons. It delays the next prompt and raises an alert instead, because an operator locked out mid-flight is a far worse outcome than a guessed PIN. The AMP records that setting.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-8, IA-2(1), IA-2(2), IA-2(8), IA-2(12), IA-5(1), AC-7. SIP record: [ID-2.1](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-21-user-authentication-controls). Details: the AMP, [Section 2](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#2-authentication-policy) and [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-2.2: Credential Management

KESTREL checks the credentials people carry, but it does not issue them. DoD issues the CACs, and the program office sponsors performers' cards through DoD's contractor sponsorship system, asking for revocation the day someone leaves. IT Operations will reset CAC PINs at dedicated workstations in the data center and at each operating site. A lost card gets no stand-in credential, and its holder waits for a replacement.

Devices and workloads are another matter. Their certificates come from the program PKI, whose keys sit in the nShield HSMs, and Keyfactor Command manages them in every location. Revocation checks have to tolerate an outage, so services accept a cached response for up to 24 hours. The stations go further and keep a local list, refreshed daily and before each flight. Any outage longer than the AMP's grace period falls to break-glass.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-5, IA-5(2). SIP record: [ID-2.2](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-22-credential-management). Details: the AMP, [Section 2](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#2-authentication-policy).</sub>

### ID-2.3: Single Sign on (SSO)

Analysts and operators will sign in once and reach the mission applications from there. In the cloud, applications from the analyst portal to the LLM analyst assistant federate with Entra ID. They use OIDC wherever possible, and SAML only where a COTS product offers nothing else. Data center applications federate with AD FS on the on-premises directory instead, so they keep working if the circuit fails.

Administrative consoles are kept out of that shared session, and each one asks for fresh authentication. Partner systems sit outside single sign-on entirely, since they reach the partner API with mutual TLS, as Server and Services Authentication describes.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-2(10), SI-10, SI-10(5). SIP record: [ID-2.3](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-23-single-sign-on-sso). Details: the AMP, [Section 8](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#8-sso-and-federation).</sub>

### ID-2.4: Non-Privileged Access Control

A new identity will start with no access at all, and roles are what grant it. Non-privileged roles are Active Directory groups, synchronized to Entra ID, and every role includes the holder's team. That one detail keeps the payload vendor split intact. An analyst on one mission team has no role that reaches the other team's vendor data.

Partners get the narrowest view. Their release-by-nation groups reach only the partner API, so each partner sees only what has been released to its own nation. Anyone who has not signed in sees nothing but the banner and the sign-in pages.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-3(7), AC-3, AC-6, AC-14. SIP record: [ID-2.4](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-24-non-privileged-access-control). Details: the AMP, [Section 4](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#4-account-lifecycle) and [Section 5](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#5-role-based-access-control-rbacgbac-model) and [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-2.5: Adaptive, Risk-Based Access Control

Before granting access, Entra Conditional Access will weigh identity alongside device posture, network origin, and risk. In practice, a performer reaches the identity-aware proxy or a VDI pool only from a laptop that reports as compliant at that moment. Program office staff are held to the same test on the parent organization's managed devices.

Network origin comes from the Boundary Cloud Access Point, and a partner call from outside that nation's expected networks is refused. Entra ID Protection feeds its risk signal into every decision. In Phase 3, badge correlation will join it as one more signal.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-3(13), AC-2(11). SIP record: [ID-2.5](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-25-adaptive-risk-based-access-control). Details: the AMP, [Section 7](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#7-session-and-risk-based-access).</sub>

### ID-2.6: Continuous Authentication

KESTREL will keep checking sessions after sign-in. Cloud and VDI sessions are re-evaluated as they run, under continuous access evaluation and the AMP's timeouts, and a session is revoked if its risk turns severe. Each account type also has a limit on concurrent sessions, tighter for privileged accounts, and going over it raises an alert.

The ground control stations are the exception. A station locks after 15 minutes of inactivity, except while its aircraft is airborne, when it neither locks nor logs the operator out. CCSD tailoring action 2 records that decision. Both station rules take effect when the fleet integrates in Phase 3.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-12, IA-11, SC-23, IA-10, AC-11, AC-10, AC-2(5). SIP record: [ID-2.6](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-26-continuous-authentication). Details: the AMP, [Section 7](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#7-session-and-risk-based-access).</sub>

## ID-3: Non-Person Entity Identity Protection

Many of the identities in KESTREL belong to workloads, pipelines, services, two AI agents, the aircraft, and the stations rather than to people. The design avoids stored secrets wherever the platform can vouch for a workload. Cloud services will therefore use native workload identities, while the few on-premises services without a native identity will use governed accounts with certificates.

### ID-3.1: Cloud Workload Identities

In the cloud, no service should need a stored secret to reach the data it uses. Every IL5 workload will therefore use the platform's native identity, either AKS workload identity or a managed identity federated to Entra ID, scoped to its own spoke. Azure Machine Learning compute and Container Instances groups take managed identities as well. With those in place, services read the data lake zones, the report index, and the model endpoints without holding any credential. The on-premises data lake accepts the same federated tokens.

Pipelines get identities of their own, with tighter limits. A team's runner reaches only that team's dev/test spoke, and only the protected release runner can deploy to a release target. Any static credential that turns up in a cloud spoke is removed once a native identity can take its place.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-9, AC-6, IA-5(7). SIP record: [ID-3.1](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-31-cloud-workload-identities).</sub>

### ID-3.2: Application and Service Account Identities

A few services in the data center and at the alternate site cannot use a native identity, and they are the only ones that will get service accounts. Where possible, each will be a group Managed Service Account, whose password Windows manages. The rest authenticate with a program PKI certificate. In both cases, the account is requested through the service desk and has a named owner.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-9, AC-6, IA-5(2), AC-2(3). SIP record: [ID-3.2](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-32-application-and-service-account-identities). Details: the AMP, [Section 4](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#4-account-lifecycle).</sub>

### ID-3.3: AI Agent Identities

Each AI agent will have an identity of its own, an Entra workload identity on AKS in the spoke that runs it. That identity reaches only the tools its use case approves. The first two agents arrive in Phase 3. The mission-planning agent drafts flight plans, and the coding agent opens merge requests. Each acts for the user who started its session, each session ends at a fixed limit, and neither calls a tool server outside the boundary.

Both agents combine untrusted input, sensitive data, and the ability to change something. Because that combination makes an agent high risk, the AO accepts each agent's scope before it acts, on the strength of a different safeguard for each. The planning agent writes only drafts, an operator approves every one, and a deterministic check holds each plan to approved areas and airspace. The coding agent works in a sandbox with no path to the internet and no credential, and nothing it pushes merges until a person has reviewed it. Each tool approval expires after a year and has to be renewed.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-6, AU-10, AC-3(2), AC-12, SA-9. SIP record: [ID-3.3](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-33-ai-agent-identities). Details: the AMP, [Section 4](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#4-account-lifecycle) and [Section 7](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#7-session-and-risk-based-access).</sub>

### ID-3.4: Server and Services Authentication

From Phase 2, KESTREL's own services will authenticate to each other with mutual TLS, using program PKI certificates. That includes traffic across the circuits and into the feedback endpoints that accept IL6 products, where an unauthenticated caller would be most dangerous. Inside the clusters, the Istio service mesh issues the workload certificates from an intermediate under the program PKI. Data center services get theirs from Keyfactor Command.

Each internal service trusts only the program's own issuing authorities. The partner API is the one place that trusts more, since it also accepts the partner and ECA issuers on the external trust list. Elsewhere, provider-managed services authenticate callers by workload identity. User-facing edge services, for their part, present DoD PKI server certificates that browsers and partner systems already trust.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-9, SC-17. SIP record: [ID-3.4](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-34-server-and-services-authentication). Details: the AMP, [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-3.5: Secrets and Credentials Detection

KESTREL will scan for exposed secrets in every place they could leak. From Phase 2, GitLab Secret Detection scans the repositories, pipeline logs, and container images on every build and on a schedule. Defender for Cloud covers cloud storage, and the service desk tickets are scanned too, since users sometimes paste credentials into them. Beyond the boundary, GitGuardian watches public sources for any KESTREL credential. A secret found in a release candidate fails Certification to Field outright.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-5(7), SI-4. SIP record: [ID-3.5](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-35-secrets-and-credentials-detection).</sub>

### ID-3.6: Secrets and Credentials Protection

Every cloud secret will live in its own spoke's Key Vault, and nowhere else. Key Vault rotates each one automatically, and because no vault holds another team's secrets, a compromise in one spoke stays there. Secrets for the data center, the alternate site, and the fleet go into CyberArk instead.

The most sensitive keys are held in neither. The datalink and root signing keys, CCSD row 13, stay in the nShield HSMs and the datalink crypto modules, because their High confidentiality calls for hardware protection.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-5(6), IA-5(7). SIP record: [ID-3.6](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-36-secrets-and-credentials-protection). Details: the AMP, [Section 3](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#3-credential-and-secret-rotation) and [Section 9](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#9-developer-secrets-workflow).</sub>

### ID-3.7: OT/Legacy Device Identity Controls

Before any fleet equipment is fielded, its vendor-default credentials will be removed from the aircraft, stations, launch and recovery equipment, and operating site services. Each aircraft and station then authenticates on the datalinks with a program PKI device identity, loaded with the manufacturer's tools, and those credentials rotate in maintenance windows.

Some equipment cannot authenticate itself, such as launch and recovery gear with fixed controllers. That equipment is identified by where it sits in the zone and conduit design. Fleet Operations will prove the approach on the spares in Phase 2, then apply it across the fleet in Phase 3.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-3, IA-3(1), IA-5. SIP record: [ID-3.7](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-37-otlegacy-device-identity-controls). Details: the AMP, [Section 3](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#3-credential-and-secret-rotation).</sub>

## ID-4: Privileged Access Management

Administrative access gives an attacker the most leverage, so KESTREL will restrict it more tightly than any other access. No account will hold a standing privilege. Instead, an administrator activates a role for a bounded window, and the session that uses it is brokered and recorded. Tier 0, which covers the directory, the PKI, and the HSMs, has an added restriction. It can be administered only from physical workstations in the data center and at the alternate site.

### ID-4.1: Privileged Access Control

Privileged roles will be defined for each administrative surface. The surfaces are the cloud hub, each spoke, the cluster control planes, the data center, the alternate site, the PKI and HSMs, and the ground segment. Entra Privileged Identity Management holds the cloud roles, and CyberArk holds the rest. No single role is allowed to span both the HSMs and the cloud tenants.

Ownership follows the systems. Each team holds the roles for what it runs, so Fleet Operations administers the ground segment. A team gets cloud administrative roles only once it runs its own production spoke. Tier 0 roles go only to the named Tier 0 administrators. The Security Team and the CSSP mostly read and audit. Their few exceptions are spelled out, such as the detection content role, which deploys rules through the pipeline.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-3(7), AC-6(5), AC-2(7), AC-6(10). SIP record: [ID-4.1](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-41-privileged-access-control). Details: the AMP, [Section 5](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#5-role-based-access-control-rbacgbac-model) and [its appendix](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#appendix-reference-catalogs-and-configuration-data).</sub>

### ID-4.2: Privileged Access Workstations and Administrative Tiering

Administrative access will also depend on the device it comes from. Tier 0 and the cloud tenant-owner roles will be administered only from physical privileged access workstations in the data center and at the alternate site. These run Windows 11 Enterprise, hardened to the DISA STIG. Other Tier 1 work runs from the Platform Team's Azure Virtual Desktop host pool.

That host pool is reached from performer laptops KESTREL does not own, which is a known weakness. The broker is built to compensate for it. It checks the CAC and the laptop's posture, allows elevation only inside the session, records everything, and lets a reviewer end a session live. Smart card redirection is allowed, while clipboard, drive, and USB redirection are blocked. Anyone who works across tiers also holds a separate account for each one.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-6(2), AC-6(3), SC-2. SIP record: [ID-4.2](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-42-privileged-access-workstations-and-administrative-tiering). Details: the AMP, [Section 10](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#10-privileged-access-management).</sub>

### ID-4.3: Just in Time Access

No privilege in KESTREL will be standing. Every cloud, data center, and ground segment privilege is instead eligible, and an administrator activates it only for a bounded window. Cloud roles are activated through Entra Privileged Identity Management, while on-premises and fleet roles go through CyberArk. The PKI and HSMs carry extra weight, so activating access to them needs a second approver.

For Tier 1, elevation happens inside an administrative VDI session. The credentials and tokens it produces therefore stay in that session and never reach the performer's laptop.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-2(6). SIP record: [ID-4.3](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-43-just-in-time-access). Details: the AMP, [Section 10](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#10-privileged-access-management).</sub>

### ID-4.4: Privileged Credential Vaulting and Session Brokering

Appliances ship with built-in administrative accounts that attackers commonly target. CyberArk will vault these accounts on the HSMs, network appliances, hypervisors, out-of-band controllers, database engines, and the ground segment. Every session that uses one is brokered and recorded, and a reviewer can watch it live or end it.

A handful of actions are serious enough to need two people every time. They are HSM key ceremonies, fleet counter-signing, root CA operations, deleting audit records, and changing a cloud tenant's security settings. CyberArk's dual control enforces most of them, and the nShield card quorum enforces HSM key operations.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: IA-5(6), AC-2(9), IA-2(5), AC-3(2), AU-14, AU-14(3), SI-4(20), AC-17(4). SIP record: [ID-4.4](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-44-privileged-credential-vaulting-and-session-brokering). Details: the AMP, [Section 10](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#10-privileged-access-management).</sub>

### ID-4.5: OT/Legacy Scheduled Maintenance-Window Access

Maintenance on the fleet will happen only in scheduled windows, starting in Phase 3. Each operating site will have a weekly window, opened against an approved change record, and covering the ground control stations, launch equipment, and aircraft. The one firm rule is that no window opens while an aircraft under its stations is airborne. Extending a window needs both Fleet Operations' operations lead and an ISSO.

Tools are inspected before they are used. Model packages also load only during these windows, which ties maintenance to the path that carries new edge models to the aircraft.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-2(2), AC-2(6), MA-2, MA-3(1), MA-3(2), MA-5. SIP record: [ID-4.5](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-45-otlegacy-scheduled-maintenance-window-access). Details: the AMP, [Section 10](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#10-privileged-access-management).</sub>

### ID-4.6: Emergency Access

KESTREL will keep break-glass accounts for the case where normal sign-in fails. There will be break-glass accounts for the cloud tenant, the directory, and the ground segment. The two cloud accounts use different phishing-resistant methods, one a YubiKey and the other a certificate from a dedicated break-glass CA, so a single failure cannot take out both. The directory set covers a domain account, each domain controller's DSRM password, and a local administrator on each privileged access workstation. Every station has its own local account as well.

The directory and station accounts are console-only passwords under CCSD tailoring action 6, which still awaits the AO's decision. If the AO declines it, offline smart cards in the same seals take their place. Using any of these accounts alerts the Security Team and the CSSP at once, and each password is changed after use. Sessions are short, too. A directory session ends after four hours, and a station session ends once no aircraft under that station is airborne. The cloud and directory sets will be sealed at the data center and the alternate site from Phase 1. The station accounts follow at each operating site from Phase 3.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-2(2), AC-2(12), CP-13. SIP record: [ID-4.6](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-46-emergency-access). Published as the [Break-Glass Account Retrieval runbook](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Break-Glass-Account-Retrieval). Details: the AMP, [Section 11](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#11-emergency-access).</sub>

### ID-4.7: Access Process for Third-Party Support

Vendor access will run through a single controlled path. A vendor engineer connects from a dedicated host pool in Azure Virtual Desktop, using an ECA Medium Hardware credential. Even then, the session must be for an open Jira Service Management case that the system-owning team lead sponsors. CyberArk brokers and records every session. No session lasts longer than eight hours, and each one ends when its case closes.

Fleet vendors face one more limit, which is the maintenance window. Within it, they either work on site under escort or connect through the same brokered path.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: MA-4, MA-4(1), AC-2(2), PS-7, AC-17(1). SIP record: [ID-4.7](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-47-access-process-for-third-party-support). Details: the AMP, [Section 12](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan#12-third-party-and-vendor-access).</sub>

## ID-5: Account Management Planning

The narratives above explain how identity will work. The Account Management Plan (AMP) holds the specific values behind them, such as assurance levels, session limits, and review cadences. Keeping those values in one plan means a change is made once, and a monthly reconciliation will check that the live systems still match it.

### ID-5.1: Account Management Plan (AMP)

All of the identity decisions above come together in one Account Management Plan. It covers every identity population KESTREL has, from people and partners to AI agents and OT devices, across the cloud, the data center, the alternate site, and the fleet. In it are the assurance levels, the role bundles, the maintenance-window rules, and the break-glass procedures.

The plan also explains the station exceptions in one place, which matters because they are easy to misread out of context. Those are the lock exception under CCSD tailoring action 2, no lockout or idle logout while an aircraft is airborne, and the revocation grace period. The Security Team's ISSM owns the plan and the Configuration Control Board approves it. Because it names the products the Security Implementation Plan selects, its procedures can be followed as written.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: AC-1, IA-1. SIP record: [ID-5.1](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-51-account-management-plan-amp). Published as the [Account Management Plan](https://github.com/jessestarkey/Kestrel/wiki/Account-Management-Plan).</sub>

### ID-5.2: AMP Compliance Verification

KESTREL will check that the live systems match the AMP. From Phase 2, a monthly reconciliation in Splunk will compare Entra ID, Active Directory, and CyberArk against the AMP. When the fleet integrates in Phase 3, the ground control stations' account settings join the comparison. Any drift goes to the ISSM, who tracks each finding in Jira and in eMASS until it closes.

<sub>**Planned.** Controls: CA-7. SIP record: [ID-5.2](../04-sip/02-identity.md#id-52-amp-compliance-verification).</sub>
